contentHtml:
Dr R Kishore Kumar, Founder Chairman, Cloudnine Group of Hospitals and President, National Neonatology Forum, Karnataka Chapter, discusses why prevention, early intervention and stronger healthcare systems are essential to reducing the burden of childhood pneumonia

Pneumonia is often treated as “just another cough” until a child begins struggling to breathe. But at a public-health level, pneumonia represents something much bigger: a preventable cause of childhood death that exposes gaps in nutrition, immunisation, air quality, sanitation and access to timely healthcare. The latest global estimates show that lower respiratory infections, including pneumonia, accounted for around 13 per cent of all deaths among children under five in 2024, making pneumonia one of the leading causes of childhood mortality worldwide. UNICEF estimates that pneumonia continues to kill more than 700,000 children under five every year around 2,000 children every day, or one child every 43 seconds.

What makes this particularly concerning is that most pneumonia deaths are preventable.

This is why the conversation around childhood pneumonia needs to move beyond “watch for cough and fever” and towards a larger public-health question: Why are children still dying from a disease that can often be prevented, diagnosed and treated?

Pneumonia is also a disease of inequality

A child’s risk of severe pneumonia is not determined by biology alone. UNICEF describes childhood pneumonia as a “disease of inequality”, with mortality strongly associated with undernutrition, unsafe water and sanitation, household and outdoor air pollution and inadequate access to healthcare.

This means the burden does not fall equally on every child. A child living in a well-ventilated, smoke-free home, receiving adequate nutrition, timely vaccinations and prompt medical attention has access to layers of protection. Another child may be exposed to household smoke, malnutrition, overcrowding and delayed healthcare — all factors that can increase vulnerability. Pneumonia therefore cannot be tackled only inside a hospital. It has to be addressed inside homes, communities, schools and primary healthcare systems.

India has made progress — but the work is far from over

India has made substantial progress in reducing childhood mortality. The under-five mortality rate fell from 127 deaths per 1,000 live births in 1990 to 26.6 in 2024, according to UNICEF data. But progress in child survival should not obscure the remaining burden. India’s own health-system data show that among children under five admitted to health facilities with pneumonia, the case-fatality rate was 2.3% in 2023. The WHO-linked national review notes that this remained above India’s 2025 target of 1% and highlights the importance of timely care-seeking and quality pneumonia management.

That statistic is a reminder that getting a sick child to a healthcare facility early can be as important as preventing the infection in the first place.

Prevention starts before the infection

Public-health prevention begins with interventions that may appear simple but have enormous impact: vaccination, breastfeeding, adequate nutrition, clean air, hygiene and access to primary healthcare. WHO identifies immunisation, adequate nutrition and reduction of environmental risk factors among the key measures for preventing childhood pneumonia.

Breastfeeding deserves particular attention. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months provides nutrition as well as immune-protective components, while appropriate complementary feeding after six months supports continued growth and immune function.

Malnutrition is particularly important because a poorly nourished child is less equipped to fight infections and is at greater risk of severe illness. WHO notes that nutrition-related factors contribute to approximately 45% of deaths among children under five, directly or indirectly. So when we talk about pneumonia prevention, we are also talking about food security, maternal education, breastfeeding support and access to nutritious food.

Vaccines are a public-health intervention, not simply an individual choice

Vaccination against pathogens such as pneumococcus, Hib, measles and pertussis can reduce the risk of pneumonia and serious complications. The pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is particularly important because pneumococcal disease is a major cause of serious childhood infections. But vaccination has a broader public-health value: high immunisation coverage reduces transmission and protects children who may be particularly vulnerable to severe disease. Every missed or delayed vaccine therefore matters not only to the individual child, but potentially to the wider community.

Clean air is child-health policy

A smoke-free home should be considered a basic requirement for healthy childhood, not simply a lifestyle preference. Children exposed to tobacco smoke and household air pollution are more vulnerable to respiratory illness. Outdoor air pollution adds another layer of exposure, particularly in heavily polluted urban environments. This makes childhood pneumonia part of the larger conversation around air-quality regulation, clean cooking fuels, tobacco control, urban planning and environmental health. If we tell parents to keep children away from polluted air but do not address the sources of that pollution, we are treating the symptom rather than the public-health problem.

The healthcare system matters too

Prevention alone will not eliminate pneumonia.

Children need to be recognised early, assessed correctly and treated promptly. WHO’s 2024 guideline specifically emphasises strengthening pneumonia management, including care at the community level and better recognition of hypoxaemia. Yet WHO estimates that only around one in three children with pneumonia receives the antibiotics they need when bacterial pneumonia requires antibiotic treatment. This highlights two problems at once: some children do not receive treatment quickly enough, while others may receive unnecessary antibiotics for illnesses that do not require them.

The answer is not indiscriminate antibiotic use. It is better diagnosis, trained healthcare workers, access to pulse oximetry where appropriate, reliable referral systems and timely treatment.

The public-health message is simple — but the solution is collective

Pneumonia should not be viewed as an unavoidable part of childhood. The evidence tells us that reducing childhood pneumonia requires more than asking parents to “be careful during winter.” It requires strong vaccination programmes, breastfeeding and nutrition support, clean-air policies, tobacco control, better living conditions, accessible primary healthcare and rapid recognition of danger signs.

And this is where public health has a critical role. A child should not have to be born into the right neighbourhood, breathe cleaner air, have better nutrition or live closer to a hospital to survive a preventable respiratory infection. The goal should not simply be to treat more children with pneumonia. The goal should be to prevent children from developing severe pneumonia in the first place — and to ensure that no child dies because prevention, recognition or treatment came too late. Pneumonia is a medical condition. But childhood pneumonia at this scale is a public-health issue. And tackling it requires action far beyond the paediatric ward — from the kitchen and classroom to the community and healthcare system.
